title: Search, rebuilt so it could be tested
standfirst: The Hotels.com app showed search results in a card framework nothing could be varied inside. Rebuilding it as dynamic cards turned the most valuable screen in the app into one the team could actually learn from.

contribution.detail: [NEEDS: your specific scope. The Apps page credits Product, Developers and Analytics as collaborators but does not say what you personally decided. On the search work: did you own the layout system, the test design, the hypotheses, or all three?]
Product, engineering and analytics, running a continuous multivariate testing programme
2018 and 2019, with the same surface revisited in 2025

problem.heading: The problem
problem.standfirst: A layout that cannot vary cannot be tested, and search results are the screen where testing matters most.
paras: Search results were built on a static card framework. Every property appeared in the same fixed arrangement, which meant that any question about what a traveller actually needed to see in order to choose was unanswerable. There was no way to put a different amount of content in front of someone and find out.

Refactoring to dynamic cards was not a visual exercise. It was about making the results page capable of holding more content, in more arrangements, so the team could run real tests on the highest traffic screen in the app.

[NEEDS: the insight, and this is the gap that matters most. What did you know about how travellers were failing on this screen? Drop-off between results and property page, scroll depth before the first tap, how many results people compared before choosing, complaints about missing information. One finding turns this from a technical refactor into a user problem, and it is the first thing a reader looks for.]

process.heading: How it was worked out
process.standfirst: Three layouts, tested against each other, inside a continuous programme rather than as a one-off launch.
process.openingPara: Three adaptive layouts were built and tested against each other. The work sat inside an ongoing multivariate testing programme run jointly by product, design, engineering and analytics, so a change did not ship on judgement and then get defended. It shipped as a hypothesis and either survived contact with real traffic or did not.

principle._note: One paragraph, three editable parts, because the middle is emphasised. Editing is plain text, so a <strong> inside a single string would be stripped the first time anyone touched it.
principle.before: The operating principle, in your words at the time:
principle.quote: create a hypothesis to give us an opportunity to learn, not to predict.
principle.after: That distinction is what makes a losing test useful rather than embarrassing, and it is why the one below was kept rather than deleted.

explorations.title: A search recap carrying check in details
explorations.why: Lost. It had a negative impact on conversion, so it went back out and was retested without the check in details. Showing a traveller a summary of what they had already told us cost more attention than it returned.

interface.heading: The flow, twice
interface.standfirst: Dynamic cards in 2019. In 2025 the same journey again, this time the movement between the two screens rather than the screens themselves.
interface.mediaAlt: The three adaptive search result layouts side by side, showing how card content varies between them
interface.mediaCaption: The dynamic card framework. Each layout carries a different amount of content in the same slot, which is what made the results page testable.
paras: Moving from static to dynamic cards changed what the card was. Instead of a fixed arrangement of a fixed set of fields, it became a container the team could vary: more content where it earned attention, less where it did not, and different arrangements for different result positions.

In 2025 I came back to the same journey from the other side, prototyping the app shell transitions in Principle: search results into the property page, the loading state on results, and the movement into trips. A card that expands into the page it belongs to keeps the traveller oriented in a way a page swap does not, and on the highest traffic path in the app that orientation is the difference between comparing properties and starting over.

[NEEDS: the transitions themselves, as video or as frame sequences. Motion described in prose is the one thing that genuinely does not survive the page. If the Principle files still exist, exports of the SRP to PDP transition and the results loading state would carry this whole section.]

impact.heading: Impact
impact.standfirst: The dynamic card framework outlived the redesign that introduced it. It is what everything after it was tested inside.

metrics.label: increase in customers returning within 30 days
increase in shortlisting, the behaviour that precedes a booking
adaptive layouts tested against each other on the app's highest traffic screen

One honest candidate, if it is true: the framework was built to make testing possible, and the tests that ran through it were mostly about content and arrangement rather than about whether the results page was the right model at all. A second: the recap test lost and was retested with one variable removed, which is the right instinct, but three layouts producing one recorded outcome suggests the learning was not captured as carefully as the shipping was.]
